title: The United Arab Emirates went from deciding to build nuclear power to first grid electricity in about twelve years, with no prior nuclear industry
oneLiner: The Barakah project is the clearest recent case of a newcomer country building reactors from a standing start.
body: The UAE adopted its nuclear policy in 2008, created a regulator and a utility, selected a Korean reactor design, and connected the first of four Barakah units to the grid in 2020. It did so with imported expertise and a vendor delivering a design already operating elsewhere.
contextBackground: Barakah is cited by both sides. Proponents of nuclear point to it as proof that a newcomer can build quickly; opponents note that it relied on a non-democratic planning process, a single vendor relationship and conditions that do not transfer to Australia.
contextDisagreement: The fact is not disputed. What is disputed is whether it bears on Australia: twelve years from a 2026 start still lands in the late 2030s, so the example narrows the gap without closing it.

evidenceItems.citation: World Nuclear Association, Nuclear Power in the United Arab Emirates — country profile

otherClaim.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040

claimItself.title: A first Australian nuclear power reactor could not be generating electricity before 2040
claimItself.oneLiner: Legislation, licensing, site selection, workforce and construction each take years, and none has started.
claimItself.body: Starting from no regulator for power reactors, no licensed site and no construction supply chain, the sequence of repeal, regulatory design, licensing, approvals and a first-of-a-kind build is estimated by CSIRO and others at fifteen years or more. On that reckoning a decision taken now delivers first power around 2040 at the earliest.

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Australia has no licensing regime, construction supply chain or operating workforce for nuclear power reactors
